So of the 867 ms the pieces cost, rasterising them unlit is 100 ms (11%), lighting them over the 21 punctual lights is 133-367 ms, and the custom stone GLSL is ~400 ms ON TOP of PBR and ~767 ms over unlit — 45% of the whole frame, the single largest item left. critiqueDetail:
THE GUARANTEE IS INTACT, and it was tested against THIS round's working tree (5 files modified, 3 new, 544 insertions, including a rewritten src/pieces/index.ts and two new modules). Two wide-establishing captures at t=3 are byte-identical to each other AND to round 4's (cmp clean, md5 f64e1f7eee0c9fa66f15630a3334c5f8, 2,630,788 bytes). king-surrender at t=2.8 comes back md5 45ebe28f78b6837bb2816b5fcccbe9ab at 2,264,723 bytes — the exact hash and byte count rounds 3 and 4 recorded. verify-mate is 3/3 with zero legal replies. And there is a second, independent proof that the high tier was not touched: at 844x390 with ?quality=high it renders 229 draw calls, 858,118 triangles, 155 geometries, 32 textures and 28 programs — every single number identical to what round 4 wrote down.

BOTH DEFECTS I WAS SENT TO CHECK ARE GENUINELY FIXED, and I tried hard to break them.

1. THE ENGINE. I instrumented window.Worker from a page init script — subclassing it so construction, every postMessage, every message event, every error and every terminate is stamped — and it is emphatic: ONE worker constructed at t=7.4 s, its 'hello' received at t=11.1 s, then seven jobs posted and seven acknowledged and seven results returned. 15 message events RECEIVED. ZERO terminates. ZERO errors. Round 4 logged one job, zero message events and a terminate 7 ms after the post. Click-to-reply in real seconds across seven moves at 844x390 CSS / deviceScaleFactor 2: 1.02, 0.81, 3.78, 0.83, 5.79, 0.35, 0.81. Round 4 measured 129.8, 139.6, 140.1, 101.0, 116.2. That is 24x to 300x, and the worst case is now under six seconds. The worker's own search takes 175-411 ms. The one 5.79 s outlier is worth naming precisely, because it is the whole remaining latency story: on that move the worker's ACK alone took 5,781 ms — the search thread waited nearly six seconds for a scheduling slot on a four-core box whose main thread holds the CPU for 1.7 s at a stretch. The new watchdog (four silent frames AND 2.5 s, both required) correctly declined to condemn it, and the worker won anyway. The old eight-second wall-clock watchdog would have killed it. That is exactly the case the rewrite was for, and it was hit in a seven-move game.

2. THE SCALER. At 932x430 I sampled the render buffer every three seconds for 132 seconds: 800x369 on every one of 45 samples. Zero changes. Frame time over that window ran 1,003-1,885 ms — 14 to 27 times FRAME_SLOW — and the ladder stayed pinned to the floor, which is the correct behaviour. Round 4 watched it walk 800x369 -> 857x395 -> 932x430 -> 857x395 -> 932x430. The run-based climb gate is doing its job: a machine at 1.7 s a frame cannot produce two consecutive sub-33 ms frames, let alone the 45 the climb now demands.

THE COST WORK IS REAL BUT IT AIMED AT THE WRONG AXIS, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SO CLEANLY.

The geometry reductions are exactly what was promised. At 844x390 with no query parameters, world.quality is 'low', the buffer is 800x370 behind an 844x390 canvas, and the frame submits 93 draw calls and 139,298 triangles against round 4's 117 and 404,665 — 2.90x the triangles gone, 24 draw calls gone. 48 geometries against 80; 129 visible meshes against 212; 26 textures and 25 programs unchanged. The LOD ladder is genuinely live and all three rungs are in use at once: reading the selected geometry off every visible piece gives 16 men at level 0, 12 at level 1 and 4 at level 2. Hiding exactly the 32 visible piece groups drops 32 draw calls and 89,232 triangles, so the pieces are 64.1% of the geometry against 87.6% last round — a 3.97x cut in piece triangles specifically.

AND IT BOUGHT ALMOST NOTHING, because the frame was never triangle-bound. Hiding those same 32 groups takes the frame from 1,700 ms to 850 ms: the pieces still cost ~850 ms and are still ~50% of the frame, against 55% last round. The decisive experiment is the material swap — same geometry, same 93 draw calls, same 139,298 triangles, same pixels covered, only the fragment shader changed: shipped stone 1,717 ms, MeshStandardMaterial 1,317, MeshLambertMaterial 1,083, MeshBasicMaterial 950, pieces gone entirely 850. Rasterising all 89,232 piece triangles unlit costs 100 ms. Everything else the pieces cost — 767 ms — is per-pixel work. The custom stone GLSL alone is ~400 ms MORE than a stock PBR material, 23% of the frame, and 45% of the frame is piece shading. Confirmed independently by the resolution response through the app's own path: 850 / 1,217 / 1,767 ms at 0.116 / 0.189 / 0.314 Mpx with the triangle count held at 139,29x throughout, which is ~317 ms fixed plus 4,610 ms per megapixel — against round 4's 4,780 ms/Mpx. A 2.90x triangle cut moved the per-megapixel slope by 3.6%.

AND THE HONEST FRAME-TIME NUMBER, WHICH NEEDS A CONTROL. Raw, this box renders the low tier at a median 1,733-1,850 ms where round 4 measured 2,701 ms through the same app loop, which looks like a 1.5x win. It is not. The high tier is untouched code and returns byte-for-byte the same draw calls, triangles, geometries, textures and programs as round 4 — a perfect control — and it renders at 10,733 ms where round 4 measured 14,848 ms. This machine is simply running 1.38x faster today. Normalise round 4's low tier by that same factor and you expect ~1,953 ms; I measure 1,733-2,040 across four separate 14-to-30-frame runs. The low:high ratio went from 5.50x to 6.15x. So the defensible claim for this round's rendering work is 'the pieces went from 55% of the frame to 49%, and from 87.6% of the triangles to 64.1%' — not a 1.5x speedup. If the round's commit message claims the latter, it is claiming the weather.

IT PLAYS, AND THE POSITIONS ARE REAL CHESS. Seven moves clicked through the actual canvas at 844x390 with deviceScaleFactor 2, every one accepted, the engine answering every one, reaching 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6 3.Bc4 d5 4.d4 dxc4 5.Nc3 Nf6 6.O-O — a capture and castling on both sides included. Every position I sampled replays through a FRESH Engine with an exact FEN round-trip and 20-37 legal replies, and because the app is fast enough now that a move and its reply can land inside one rendered frame, I also proved the gaps: a make/unmake iterative-deepening search connects every consecutive pair by an explicit legal ply sequence (step 2 via 'Nc6 Nf3 e6', step 4 via 'd5 d4 dxc4 Nc3'). Zero page errors, zero console errors, across every run.

TWO SMALLER THINGS. The factory holds 64 PieceInstances for the 32 men on the board — 32 of them are permanently invisible. With the pool they share geometry so it is not a frame cost, but it is 32 live objects and 32 groups traversed every frame for nothing. And the low tier still has no shadow map (10 spot, 11 point, 1 hemisphere, 1 ambient, 0 shadow casters), which round 4 already flagged as making interactive.ts's shadow-refresh budget dead code on the tier it was written for; that was not addressed.

history.gap: none — 3/3 demo lines verified as real checkmate with zero legal replies

The play camera crops White's own back rank off the bottom of the frame — all eight rank-1 square centres sit 20-23 px below the canvas edge, leaving a 22-28 px sliver, so clicking where your own knight or king appears to be does nothing. Deterministic at every window size, and it hits on move 2.

You cannot tell what any piece is by looking at it. Every piece is the same pale armoured figure from behind and only height separates the types: rook 119.2 px, knight 132.2 px, bishop 141.1 px on screen — 13.0 px and 8.8 px apart, 7-11 percent of their own height, with no colour, crest or marking to help. It survives at full capture resolution, so it is not the software renderer. I picked all nine of my moves by reading the FEN out of the JS console; and since the HUD never prints state.lastMove, you also cannot tell what the engine just played.

The 32 carved pieces. They are 354,599 of the 404,665 triangles the phone submits every frame (87.6%), 56 of its 117 draw calls, and 1,065 ms of a 1,919 ms frame (55%) — measured by hiding exactly those 32 groups at a fixed 800x370 buffer and timing with a readPixels fence: 1,919 -> 854 ms, 117 -> 61 calls, 404,665 -> 50,066 triangles. The board, which this round rebuilt, is now 5 calls, 11,746 triangles and 296 ms; the chamber is 34 calls and 420 ms. src/pieces is the one module the round did not open. Every figure is uniquely carved, so nothing is instanced or merged; there is one body mesh plus one arm mesh per piece, no LOD of any kind, and a pawn 30 m away at the top of the frame carries the same ~11,000 triangles as the king a metre from the lens. 64 carved geometries are resident for the 32 men actually on the board.
